{{short description|Type of solvable group in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''polycyclic group''' is a [[solvable group]] that satisfies the maximal condition on [[subgroup]]s (that is, every subgroup is [[Finitely generated group|finitely generated]]). Polycyclic groups are [[finitely presented group|finitely presented]], which makes them interesting from a computational point of view.

==Terminology==
Equivalently, a group ''G'' is polycyclic if and only if it admits a [[subnormal series]] with cyclic factors, that is a finite set of subgroups, let's say ''G''<sub>0</sub>, ..., ''G''<sub>''n''</sub> such that
* ''G''<sub>''n''</sub> coincides with ''G''
* ''G''<sub>0</sub> is the trivial subgroup
* ''G''<sub>''i''</sub> is a normal subgroup of ''G''<sub>''i''+1</sub> (for every ''i'' between 0 and ''n'' - 1)
* and the quotient group ''G''<sub>''i''+1</sub> / ''G''<sub>''i''</sub> is a [[cyclic group]] (for every ''i'' between 0 and ''n'' - 1)

A [[metacyclic group]] is a polycyclic group with ''n'' ≤ 2, or in other words an [[group extension|extension]] of a cyclic group by a cyclic group.

==Examples==
Examples of polycyclic groups include finitely generated abelian groups, finitely generated [[nilpotent group|nilpotent]] groups, and finite solvable groups. [[Anatoly Maltsev]] proved that solvable subgroups of the integer [[general linear group]] are polycyclic; and later [[Louis Auslander]] (1967) and Swan proved the converse, that any polycyclic group is up to isomorphism a group of integer matrices.<ref>Dmitriĭ Alekseevich Suprunenko, K. A. Hirsch, ''Matrix groups'' (1976), pp. 174–5; [https://books.google.com/books?id=cTtuPOj5h10C&pg=PA174 Google Books].</ref> The [[holomorph (mathematics)|holomorph]] of a polycyclic group is also such a group of integer matrices.<ref>{{SpringerEOM|id=p/p073560|title=Polycyclic group}}</ref>

==Strongly polycyclic groups==

A polycyclic group ''G'' is said to be '''strongly polycyclic''' if each quotient ''G''<sub>''i''+1</sub> / ''G''<sub>''i''</sub> is infinite.  Any subgroup of a strongly polycyclic group is strongly polycyclic.

==Polycyclic-by-finite groups==

A '''virtually polycyclic group''' is a group that has a polycyclic subgroup of finite [[index (group theory)|index]], an example of a [[virtually|virtual]] property. Such a group necessarily has a ''normal'' polycyclic subgroup of finite index, and therefore such groups are also called '''polycyclic-by-finite groups'''. Although polycyclic-by-finite groups need not be solvable, they still have many of the finiteness properties of polycyclic groups; for example, they satisfy the maximal condition, and they are finitely presented and [[residually finite group|residually finite]].

In the textbook {{harv|Scott|1964|loc=Ch 7.1}} and some papers<!-- so far none important, but Pickel 1973 NilByFin is an example-->, an '''M-group''' refers to what is now called a polycyclic-[[group extension|by]]-[[finite group]], which by Hirsch's theorem can also be expressed as a group which has a finite length subnormal series with each factor a finite group or an infinite [[cyclic group]].

These groups are particularly interesting because they are the only known examples of [[noetherian ring|Noetherian]] [[group ring]]s {{harv|Ivanov|1989}}, or group rings of finite injective dimension.{{Citation needed|date=February 2008}}

==Hirsch length==

The '''Hirsch length''' or '''Hirsch number''' of a polycyclic group ''G'' is the number of infinite factors in its subnormal series.

If ''G'' is a polycyclic-by-finite group, then the Hirsch length of ''G'' is the Hirsch length of a polycyclic [[normal subgroup]] ''H'' of ''G'', where ''H'' has finite [[Index of a group|index]] in ''G''. This is independent of choice of subgroup, as all such subgroups will have the same Hirsch length.
